lookAlikes.name: holy basil
lookAlikes.howToTellApart: Holy basil usually has more serrated, slightly hairy leaves and often purple-tinged stems; sweet basil has smoother, glossier, larger leaves and a milder anise/lemon aroma.

lookAlikes.name: lemon basil
lookAlikes.howToTellApart: Lemon basil has narrower leaves and a strong lemon scent; sweet basil has broader, ovate leaves and a sweeter, clove-anise aroma.

identificationFeatures: Potted herb with opposite, ovate, entire, glossy green leaves.
Square stems typical of the Lamiaceae family.
No flowers present; plant is in vegetative growth.
This is a desirable culinary herb, not a weed.

threat.competitiveness: Not competitive as a weed in garden settings; tender annual herb.
threat.seedsPerPlant: Not applicable; if allowed to flower, a single plant may produce hundreds to thousands of seeds.
threat.seedBankPersistenceYears: Not applicable; seeds are generally short-lived in soil under normal garden conditions.
threat.toxicityNote: Generally non-toxic to livestock and humans at culinary amounts; concentrated essential oil contains estragole and should not be ingested in large quantities.
threat.regulatoryNote: Not regulated as a noxious weed in most regions; not invasive in temperate gardens.

controlWindow.bestTiming: Not applicable; maintain as a desirable herb.
controlWindow.preventSeedSet: Not applicable; if saving seed, allow flowering; otherwise deadhead to prolong leaf harvest.

resistance.advice: Not applicable; this is a crop/herb, not a weed target. No herbicide resistance management required.

usesAndBenefits: Culinary herb used fresh or dried in many cuisines.
Medicinal: traditional use for digestion, but evidence is limited; consult a healthcare provider.
Ornamental and aromatic garden plant; attracts pollinators when allowed to flower.
Companion planting: may help repel some insect pests, though evidence varies.
Safety caveat: avoid excessive consumption of concentrated essential oil; culinary use is generally recognized as safe.
